Heating energy consumption 15-minute time-series data before and after envelope upgrades Figure 4 shows that each envelope upgrade reduces cooling energy consumption compared to the baseline. The combined upgrade package (dark blue line) consistently results in the lowest cooling energy use from 12:45 to 22:00, when cooling demand is high, indicating cumulative savings from all measures. During 0:00–12:15 and 23:30–24:00 when cooling demand is minimal or absent in the baseline model, cooling energy consumption increases after the envelope package upgrade. This increase is due to the reduced air exchange and heat loss resulting from the improved building envelope. In the baseline model, natural cooling occurred during these hours through air leakage and lower outdoor temperatures. After the upgrade, the dwelling unit becomes more airtight and better insulated, reducing passive cooling and resulting in small cooling loads in the upgraded model to maintain indoor comfort. The sudden rise in cooling energy consumption at 0:15 is driven by changes in the cooling setpoint temperature of this example dwelling unit. At 0:00, the setpoint drops from 72°F to 70°F, triggering a spike in cooling energy use from 0:00 to 0:15. Afterward, cooling energy consumption returns to normal. 9 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 4. Cooling energy consumption 15-minute time-series data before and after envelope upgrades 4.2 Stock Energy Impacts 4.2.1 Annual Stock Energy Analysis Figure 5 shows the annual site energy consumption by end use before and after the envelope package upgrades for all homes. The annual stock energy savings from the envelope package upgrade is 780 TWh, compared to a pre-upgrade average consumption of 3,454 TWh— representing a 22.6% reduction. Most savings occurred in heating and cooling end uses. These include 36% (92 TWh) electricity heating savings, 40% (458 TWh) natural gas heating savings, 37% (62 TWh) fuel oil heating savings, 36% (47 TWh) propane heating savings, 68% (15 TWh) electricity heating heat pump backup savings, 21% (80 TWh) electricity cooling savings, 39% (14 TWh) electricity heating fans and pumps savings, and 20% (13 TWh) electricity cooling fans and pumps savings. 10 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Annual site energy consumption for all homes Figure 6 shows the annual site energy consumption per dwelling unit by end use before and after the envelope package upgrades for upgraded dwelling units, which include 97.9% of all dwelling units.
